title: The Real Cost of the U.S.-Canada Trade Breakdown | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: After U.S.-Canada trade talks collapsed, Trump is using the never-before-tested Section 338 to override USMCA and impose 50% tariffs on Canadian autos and steel from January 2027, with Canada retaliating dollar-for-dollar. CFR's Brad Setser argues the direct tariff cost is small but the breakdown signals a durable erosion of North American tariff-free trade and a structural problem: high U.S. tariffs make Canada/Mexico backdoors around the tariff wall, especially for Chinese autos.

insights.claim: The out-of-pocket cost of the new U.S. 50 percent tariff on Canadian goods is about $10 billion, less than a twentieth of a percentage point of U.S. GDP, so the direct hit to the U.S. economy is small absent further escalation.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: The headline tariff is macro-immaterial for the U.S.; the risk to price is escalation, not the base levy, so watch the retaliation cycle rather than the initial number.
insights.quote: The out-of-pocket cost of the new 50 percent tariff is $10 billion, which isn’t nothing, but it is small relative to the overall U.S. economy—less than a twentieth of a percentage point of U.S. GDP.
insights.locator: How much economic damage could this cause

insights.claim: Trump will raise tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel to 50 percent on January 1, 2027, and Canada's PM Mark Carney will match dollar-for-dollar with retaliatory levies on U.S. steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, and other goods beginning September 8, 2026.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Concrete dates and sectors let investors position ahead of the September 8 Canadian retaliation and the January 2027 auto/steel escalation.
insights.locator: President Donald Trump laid out the administration’s next move

insights.claim: Canada's economy is roughly one-twelfth the size of the U.S. economy and its geography complicates finding alternative markets, so the tariff damage falls far more heavily on Canada than on the United States.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Asymmetric exposure means Canadian assets and CAD carry the bulk of the trade-war risk premium, not U.S. ones.
insights.locator: The effect on Canada will, of course, be much larger

insights.claim: U.S. tariffs on primary aluminum imports from Canada pushed the U.S. aluminum price well above the global price without boosting U.S. production, because the U.S. market cannot clear without Canadian primary aluminum.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Aluminum tariffs are a cost tax on U.S. downstream manufacturers with no reshoring payoff—bearish for U.S. aluminum-consuming industries.
insights.quote: The U.S. aluminum market doesn’t clear without primary aluminum imports from Canada, so the tariff pushed the U.S. price of aluminum well above the global price.
insights.locator: The proposed deal would have brought down some of the earlier tariffs

insights.claim: New U.S. aluminum smelting investment cannot compete with hyperscalers that are bidding up the price of the electricity that new smelters would need.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: AI data-center power demand is now a structural barrier to energy-intensive reshoring—tariffs alone can't rebuild smelting when compute is outbidding it for power.
insights.quote: new investment in aluminum cannot compete with the hyperscalers that are bidding up the price of needed electricity
insights.locator: The proposed deal would have brought down some of the earlier tariffs

themes.theme: Section 338 legal tool and USMCA erosion

insights.claim: The Trump administration is using Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a dormant authority that has literally never been used before and is legally untested, with a decent chance courts rule the administration overstepped its authority.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Legal challenge risk means the 338 tariffs could be struck down like IEEPA was—an option-value catalyst for Canada-exposed trades.
insights.quote: Section 338 is also legally untested—it literally has never been used before—and there is a decent chance the courts rule that the Trump administration has overstepped its legal authority.
insights.locator: Section 338 in theory provides the legal basis

insights.claim: The USMCA was already functionally dead because Section 232 national security tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, and trucks had ended open tariff-free trade in key sectors, putting the U.S. in violation of its USMCA commitments before Section 338 was invoked.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Do not price USMCA as a live guarantee of tariff-free North American trade—it is already breached and eroding.
insights.quote: The USMCA was already functionally dead in many ways.
insights.locator: The USMCA was already functionally dead

insights.claim: The escalation ladder will produce a progressive reduction in tariff-free trade between the U.S. and Canada, as 338 tariffs answer Canadian measures taken after the 232 tariffs and Canada again retaliates.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Trend is toward less, not more, North American trade openness—structurally negative for integrated cross-border supply chains.
insights.locator: The end result will be a progressive reduction

themes.theme: Structural flaw: FTA vs customs union and the China backdoor

insights.claim: USMCA is a traditional free trade agreement that does not limit each member's tariffs on third parties, unlike a customs union such as the EU with a common external tariff—so Canada can extend tariff-free trade to China while the U.S. keeps high China tariffs.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: The FTA-vs-customs-union distinction is the core tension driving the dispute; watch for U.S. demands for aligned external tariffs (a customs-union move).
insights.locator: The USMCA is a traditional free trade agreement

insights.claim: In a world of high U.S. tariffs, producing goods in Mexico or Canada using imported parts from heavily tariffed countries has become an obvious way around the U.S. tariff wall.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Tariff arbitrage through North American assembly is the mechanism the U.S. now wants to close—exposure for firms routing Chinese content via Mexico/Canada.
insights.quote: producing goods in Mexico or Canada with imported parts from countries that the United States heavily tariffed has become an obvious way around the U.S. tariff wall
insights.locator: But now U.S. tariffs are relatively high

insights.claim: China now makes roughly one in four new cars sold in Mexico, with General Motors making cars in China for sale in Mexico and Chinese brands holding substantial share, while Canada allows only a limited number of Chinese cars.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Mexico is the live channel for Chinese autos into North America—the next flashpoint for U.S. tariff pressure and USMCA renegotiation.
insights.quote: China now makes roughly one in four new cars sold in Mexico.
insights.locator: And concretely, the United States has high tariffs

insights.claim: Canada was reportedly open to a Fortress North America with tariffs aligned against outside countries, but only if the U.S. completely dropped its current auto, steel, and aluminum tariffs on Canada, which Trump refused.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: A grand bargain exists in outline (aligned external tariffs for dropped internal tariffs); the sticking point is Trump's unwillingness to give up leverage.
insights.locator: The New York Times has reported

themes.theme: Oil flow spared and spillover to other allies

insights.claim: Neither the U.S. nor Canada has restricted the four million barrels a day of oil that Canada sends south, the biggest trade flow between the two countries.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Cross-border oil is the deliberately untouched line; any move to restrict it would be a major escalation signal for energy markets.
insights.quote: neither side has restricted the biggest trade flow between Canada and the United States: the four million barrels a day of oil that Canada sends south
insights.locator: For now, though, neither side has restricted

insights.claim: Canada is the first U.S. ally to accept real economic pain rather than give in to tariff pressure, and Brussels is watching Ottawa closely as it weighs its own posture.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Canada is a precedent test—if it endures the pain, other allies may harden, raising the odds of coordinated retaliation against U.S. tariffs.
insights.quote: Canada is the first U.S. ally to accept real economic pain rather than give in to tariff pressure.
insights.locator: Canada is the first U.S. ally

insights.claim: The EU is committed for now to its flat 15 percent U.S. tariff deal, but Setser expects Brussels to rip up the deal and retaliate if the U.S. proceeds with tariff threats over pharmaceutical pricing or digital regulation.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: The EU deal is conditional—pharma-pricing and digital-reg tariff threats are the specific triggers that would blow it up.
insights.locator: If the United States goes ahead with various existing tariff threats

insights.claim: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariff authority, potentially lowering the EU's effective U.S. tariff rate below the negotiated 15 percent.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: IEEPA being struck down is a live legal fact that resets effective tariff rates and strengthens the case that Section 338 could also fall.
insights.quote: or lower, after the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA
insights.locator: preferring the certainty of a flat 15 percent

insights.claim: Canada's trade surplus with the U.S. is not nearly as large as Mexico's or Vietnam's, and Setser warns the U.S. may later seek to change the terms of other second-term trade deals, risking further retaliation cycles.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Mexico and Vietnam, with bigger surpluses, are the more likely next targets—position for serial trade-deal reopenings, not a one-off.
